title: Excel COUNTIF Function: How to Count Cells with Criteria
description: Learn how to use the Excel COUNTIF function to count cells that match a condition. See formula examples for text, numbers, cell references, and wildcards.

args.name: range
args.text: The group of cells you want to evaluate.

args.name: criteria
args.text: The condition that determines which cells to count. Can be a number, text, cell reference, comparison expression, or wildcard pattern.

sections.heading: Count cells that match specific text
sections.text: Use **COUNTIF** to count cells containing an exact word or text string. Text comparisons in Excel are case-insensitive, so `"Apples"` and `"apples"` match the same cells. Always enclose text criteria in double quotes.

sections.heading: Count numbers with greater than or less than
sections.text: To count numbers above or below a threshold, combine a comparison operator with your number inside quotation marks. For example, use `">=50"` to include values equal to 50, or `"<20"` to find smaller values.

sections.heading: Use a cell reference for dynamic criteria
sections.text: You can supply criteria from another cell instead of hardcoding a value. Do not put quotation marks around the cell reference. If the criterion cell changes, your count updates automatically.

sections.heading: Count partial matches with wildcards
sections.text: Use wildcards when you only know part of the text. An asterisk `*` matches any number of characters, and a question mark `?` matches any single character. To count cells that contain a keyword anywhere inside, place an asterisk on both sides, such as `"*Report*"`.

sections.heading: Common mistake: missing quotes on comparisons
sections.text: A frequent mistake is omitting quotes around comparison operators, writing `=COUNTIF(B2:B6, >=50)` instead of `=COUNTIF(B2:B6, ">=50")`. Excel flags unquoted operators as syntax errors. If you need to combine an operator with a cell reference such as `C1`, join them using an ampersand: `">="&C1`.
